question.leadin: Answer the following about "dreams" in American history.
question.text: Mahalia Jackson prompted this civil rights leader to "Tell them about the dream" during his "I Have a Dream" speech as part of the March on Washington.
question.clue: Robert Kennedy's impromptu speech in Indianapolis following this man's death probably kept the city from rioting.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about American women's history.
swap.text: This constitutional amendment, first proposed in 1923, would ban sex-based discrimination. Although Virginia became the thirty-eighth state to ratify this amendment in January 2020, it has not yet been added to the constitution.
swap.clue: This legislation failed to pass since only 35 ratified it by 1979.

question.leadin: Give the following about the presidential Election of 1948.
question.text: In the election, racist Strom Thurmond ran with this third party, whose common nickname is a mashup of"Democrat" and a term for the South. This party's official name was a political concept commonly cited inarguments for nineteenth-century slavery and twentieth-century segregation.
question.clue: Strom Thurmond won four states running on the platform of this party, nicknamed for its southern origin. This party supported a bunch of segregationist policies.

swap.text: This future Supreme Court justice argued before the Court for the NAACP in Brown v. Board of Education.
swap.clue: Earlier, he argued for the winning side of the Supreme Court cases Smith v. Allwright and Sweatt v. Painter.

question.leadin: This man gave the "Ballot or the Bullet" speech and claimed "We didn't land on Plymouth Rock. The Rock was landed on us."
question.text: Name this Civil Rights leader, who was assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom in 1965. This activist changed his last name from Little, which he called a "slave master name."
question.answerHtml: Malcolm X [accept el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, prompt on Malcolm and X]
question.clue: In a speech, this man stated that "you sure don't catch hell 'cause you're an American . . . you catch hell because you're a black man."

swap.leadin: In order to coordinate the "War on Poverty" as part of this initiative, the Office of Economic Opportunity was established.
swap.text: Name this initiative launched by a Democratic president to reduce poverty and inequality. This initiative led to the establishment of Medicare and Medicaid to provide health insurance to the elderly and the poor, respectively.
swap.clue: This plan was depicted as an improvement on being just "rich" or "powerful" in a speech at the University of Michigan in 1964.

question.text: Before eventually becoming a Supreme Court justice, Thurgood Marshall argued this case before the court. This landmark case overruled Plessy v. Ferguson by overturning the "separate but equal" doctrine.
question.clue: This case's decision cited an experiment in which children were asked to choose between dolls by Kenneth and Mamie Clark.

swap.text: Eleanor Roosevelt worked with this man in attempting to pass the Costigan-Wagner Bill, which would have made lynchings a federal crime. This activist worked with Asa Phillip Randolph to lobby for Executive Order 8802, which prohibited racial discrimination in the defense industry.
swap.clue: This first secretary of the Socialist Unity Party from 1950 to 1971, who became the de facto leader of his country after the SED set up the Council of State. He also developed the New Economic System in 1963.

question.leadin: Answer these questions concerning Supreme Court cases.
question.text: The final decision of this much debated 1954 Supreme Court case found that racial discrimination in the public schools of Washington D.C. denied blacks due process of law as protected by the Fifth Amendment and was therefore unconstitutional.
question.clue: This 1954 decision was a companion case to Brown v. Board of Education and banned segregation in Washington D.C. public schools.

swap.leadin: This politician took steam baths to dehydrate himself before delivering a speech in which he read the entirety of each state's election laws.
swap.text: Name this long-serving Senator from South Carolina whose 24 hour filibuster was unable to prevent the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
swap.clue: His loss to Olin Johnston would be the only statewide election he would ever lose.

question.leadin: This group's name was changed by leader H. Rap Brown.
question.text: Name this group also led by men such as Stokely Carmichael. It organized such campaigns as "Freedom Summer," which challenged unequal voting rights.
question.answerHtml: SNCC ["Snick"; or Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee; or Student National Coordinating Committee]
question.clue: This civil-rights organization once led by Stokely Carmichael. This organization was founded by students, and it led the Freedom Rides.

swap.text: This case, a precursor to Miranda, saw the introduction of the idea of "an absolute right to remain silent." It also guaranteed the right to have counsel present during police interregation.
swap.answerHtml: Escobedo v. Illinois [accept in reverse order, prompt on “Illinois”]
swap.clue: The phrase "absolute right to remain silent" originates in this 1964 case, which voided the confession of a man who was denied repeated requests to consult with his lawyer.

question.leadin: This speech notes "Uncle Sam's hands are dripping with blood. Dripping with the blood of the black man in this country."
question.text: Give this speech delivered less than a month after its speaker's break with the Nation of Islam. This speech was delivered at a Methodist church in Cleveland and advises African Americans to vote for change, but claims it may be necessary to take up arms if injustices continue.
question.clue: This 1964 speech by Malcolm X expressed distrust that advent of voting rights would be any different from "running from the wolf to the fox," and suggested the second titular subject may prove necessary should the first one fail.

swap.leadin: This work responded to an open letter penned by eight clergymen titled "A Call for Unity," which cautioned against "outsiders coming in."
swap.text: Name this text, which draws on Augustine in arguing that "injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere."
swap.answerHtml: “Letter from Birmingham Jail” [or “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” or “Letter from Birmingham City Jail” or “The Negro is Your Brother”]
swap.clue: It was written in response to the statement "A Call for Unity" that urged the use of the court system rather than "direct action" led by outsiders.

question.text: The decision of Keys v. Carolina Coach Co. went largely unenforced until Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy was forced to take action by these people, who rode interstate buses into the south. These people were attacked at bus stations because local police refused to protect them.
question.clue: This group of civil rights activists rode interstate buses into the deep South to test local segregation ordinances in response to the rulings in Morgan v. Virginia and Boynton v. Virginia.

swap.leadin: After the killer of this man and George Moscone only received an involuntary manslaughter conviction, the White Nights riots broke out.
swap.text: Name this California city supervisor who was killed by fellow supervisor, Dan White, whose lawyers utilized the so-called "Twinkie defense" to successfully earn a lesser conviction.
swap.clue: This man's death inspired Cleve Jones to begin the NAMES Project.

question.text: This five-term Democratic Senator won fifteen electoral votes on an independent anti-civil rights plank in the 1960 Presidential election. His "machine" controlled the state for the last forty years of segregation, and his son of the same name later won a Virginia Senate seat as an independent.
question.clue: This Virginia senator promised "massive resistance" in the face of Brown v. Board of Ed. His namesake organization dominated Virginia politics for much of the early to mid-20th century.

swap.text: This collection of essays, written in 1965 at Folsom State Prison by the one-time Minister of Information for the Black Panthers, includes three love letters to and from its author's lawyer Beverly Axelrod.
swap.clue: The Black Panther leader Eldridge Cleaver wrote this essay collection while in prison. This collection includes an allegorical reading of a Muhammad Ali fight in the context of black liberation as well as controversial homophobic and misogynist passages in its section "The Blood of the Beast."

question.leadin: Identify the following about photographs depicting racism in the US.
question.text: In this 1976 photograph by Stanley Forman, Joseph Rakes appears on the left wielding a flagpole against African-American lawyer Ted Landsmark during a protest against bussing in Boston.

swap.text: This one-time leader of the NAACP spoke at the Prayer Pilgrimage. Under his leadership, the NAACP helped black-owned businesses get loans in the South by backing the Tri-State Bank, and he eventually stepped down in 1977.
swap.clue: This activist was leader of the NAACP from 1955 to 1977, succeeding Walter White. He had earlier edited W.E.B. Du Bois's The Crisis magazine, and was known for opposing militancy in the civil rights movement.
